extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and undergraduate mathematics instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Rubric and evaluation criteria for assessing (and implementing) structured proofs and student comprehension of proofs and limit concepts in undergraduate mathematics education research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary (Level 1) comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to recognize and retain a high-quality summary of a proof provided in Level 1 of a structured proof (Level 1 gives in very general terms a description of how the proof will proceed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured-proof readers performed better on summary questions (e.g., 76% vs 63% in Only Zero; statistically reliable c(1,200)=4.095, p<0.05). But comprehension of Level 1 depends on reader familiarity and difficulty; Level 1 can be a double-edged sword—some readers may not understand the summary and thus not gain benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to apply the ideas of a proof to novel or transfer questions (questions that require applying proof ideas in new contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No evidence that structured proofs improved transfer; if anything, results suggested the linear group outperformed structured (differences not statistically reliable). Researchers should not assume structured formatting improves transfer without further evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to evaluate or produce justification steps of a proof (recognize valid justificatory moves or produce correct justifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found essentially no advantage for structured proofs on justification items; in one case the linear group did better (55% vs 40%), though not statistically reliable. Assessment items should separately probe justificatory skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration-with-examples comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to relate the ideas of a proof to specific examples or to judge whether the ideas apply to a given diagram or example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings were mixed: for Triadic Primes structured readers better at recognizing non-applicability to a graph (78% vs 69%, not reliable), but linear readers substantially better at applying the proof to a specific example (91% vs 63%; c(1,96)=9.252, p<0.01). Distinguish between recognition of non-applicability and constructive application – they are different skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-reported understanding (Likert)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants' subjective rating of 'How well do you feel you understand this proof?' recorded on a five-point Likert scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlation between self-report and cumulative comprehension scores was negative (Only Zero: -0.54; Triadic Primes: -0.185), so self-reports should not be used as a primary measure of efficacy of proof formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format liking / attitude (three-point Likert)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants' reported liking of the proof format after reading a structured proof, recorded on a three-point Likert scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing directions describing structured proofs’ nature/purpose made participants about 50% more likely to view the format positively and 50% less likely to view it negatively; directions affected attitude though not task performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured-proof format levels (presentation requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The structural conventions of a 'structured proof': Level 1 (top-level summary of how the proof proceeds), Level 2 (carrying out the arguments described in Level 1), Level 3 (logical details/computations pushed down), and 'between levels' sections (introducing ideas used later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design proofs so Level 1 provides a general sense before details; use between-levels to motivate statements. Be aware Level 1 summaries may help some readers but hinder others depending on background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental validity: discard repeat or revisiting participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological safeguard to discard participants who show evidence of participating twice (e.g., multiple submissions from same IP) or revisiting earlier pages in the study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Inglis & Mejia-Ramos (2009) methodology for web studies to reduce threats to validity in internet experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials control: avoid unrelated confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify proof texts to remove or clarify content that could cause confusion unrelated to proof format (e.g., define domain-specific terms before theorem, clarify specialized vocabulary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: define 'triadic (monadic) numbers' and clarify 'triadic (monadic) primes' before the theorem to isolate effects of format from content confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random assignment to experimental conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants should be randomly assigned to presentation conditions (e.g., LIN, S(no dir), S(w dir)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomization helps isolate format effects; if two structured conditions show no reliable differences, collapsing them into a single structured group is an analytic option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension test design and item handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Design comprehension assessments by selecting items targeting specific dimensions (summary, transfer, justification, examples); use a small number of items per proof and randomize item order per participant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items for internet study were 4–5 per proof, drawn and improved from interview study; randomize question order to reduce order effects; ensure items probe intended comprehension strands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment manipulation: provide directions describing structured proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Include explicit instructions describing the nature and purpose of structured proofs as part of the experimental manipulation when testing effects of providing directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing such directions improved participants' attitudes toward the format though it did not increase reported understanding or performance on comprehension tests in this study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical evaluation and analytic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate statistical tests to evaluate differences between conditions and make justified analytic decisions such as collapsing groups when differences are not significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report test statistics and p-values (examples: c(1,200)=4.095, p<0.05); interpret statistically reliable differences cautiously and consider post-hoc explanations for unexpected effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation guidance for instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations about implementing structured proofs in instruction: do not adopt wholesale without careful preparation, training, and evidence of learning gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues against straightforward classroom implementation without additional recommendations; suggests that extended training, careful instruction, or lecture presentation might be necessary for structured proofs to yield benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method modality (rule of four) for limits tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify students' solution methods/modalities when solving limit problems according to the 'rule of four'—graphical, algebraic (symbolic), numerical, and verbal/modal reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the rule of four as a coding/category scheme to identify the method a student uses; expect students to draw on multiple modalities across tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification type: syntactic versus semantic
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify students' justifications as syntactic (staying within symbolic context and manipulations) or semantic (moving beyond symbols to graphs, examples, tables, intuition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syntactic example: algebraic manipulation to evaluate a limit; semantic example: graphing function or using a table of values. Use this coding to interpret the nature of explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability / fit of method and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the chosen method and justification are appropriate/applicable to the given problem context (e.g., whether an example actually fits the task).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure of applicability (e.g., choosing an example that does not fit problem constraints) indicates weaker conceptual understanding even if modality or justification appears plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic decomposition stages for formal limit understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the 7-step genetic decomposition (Cottrill et al., 1996) as a descriptive tool for assessing students' grasp of the formal definition of limit (stages track progression toward formal understanding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The genetic decomposition is useful for formal-definition contexts (RME) but was not designed as a general metric outside such settings; it can be compared to students' verbalizations to infer their stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview / talk-aloud protocol and task diversity for eliciting modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use task-based interviews with a talk-aloud protocol, a variety of tasks (conceptual, unfamiliar problems, examples/non-examples), transcription, and coding for modality and justification to assess student understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design interview tasks to elicit multiple modalities (e.g., give examples/non-examples, ask for explanations, present unfamiliar limits); code transcripts for modality, justification type, and applicability to build a multi-strand model.
